reason: The chambers need muscle to squeeze, making it a direct first step toward a working pump.
expectation: The muscle will surround the chambers so they can squeeze.

effect: The chambers can squeeze, but fluid moves toward both openings, so they need a way to direct flow.
reaction: The two-way arrows make the need for valves clear.
reason: The valve picture shows cusps closing against reverse flow, directly addressing the current problem.
expectation: The valves will help direct blood forward during a squeeze.

effect: The valves direct flow during squeezing and reverse their positions during refilling. The heart still needs a way to produce repeated squeezes.
reaction: The squeeze and refill panels make the valves' roles clear.
reason: The pacemaker cells produce a spreading electrical wave, suggesting they can coordinate repeated heartbeats.
expectation: The pacemaker cells will help the heart squeeze repeatedly.

effect: The pacemaker completes the beating pump; the remaining goal is to fit it and blood into a returning route.
reaction: The distinction between starting the beat and nerves adjusting it is interesting.
reason: Hemoglobin fits inside the red-cell envelopes to make oxygen-carrying cells.
expectation: The envelopes will contain hemoglobin and form oxygen-carrying red cells.

effect: The red cells contain hemoglobin and make ATP from sugar without mitochondria; they can now be added to plasma to make blood.
reaction: The contrast with the muscle cells is interesting.
reason: Plasma is the fluid component available to carry the red blood cells.
expectation: The red cells will be suspended in plasma to form blood.

effect: The blood now contains red cells in plasma, with sugar dissolved in the fluid.
reaction: The picture clarifies where the oxygen carrier and sugar are located.
reason: Capillary networks can connect the branching arteries and veins into a route through tissues.
expectation: The capillaries will link the arteries and veins into a returning vessel route.

effect: The capillaries connect the arteries and veins, and the circuit has slots for the pump and transport medium.
reaction: The marked slots make the remaining assembly clear.
reason: The beating heart is the pump needed by the vessel circuit.
expectation: The heart will fit into the pump slot.

effect: The beating heart is installed in the vessel circuit; the transport-medium slot remains to be filled.
reaction: The remaining slot makes the next step clear.
reason: Oxygen-carrying blood is the transport medium for the circuit.
expectation: The blood will fill the transport-medium slot and complete the returning route.

effect: The blood completes the circuit, showing tissue exchange and blood returning to circulate again.
reaction: The capillary inset usefully connects the completed route to the cells it supplies.

mostWorthwhile.text: Completing the circuit was most worthwhile because it connected the pump, blood and vessels to exchange with tissues and showed blood returning for another circuit.

leastWorthwhile.text: Installing the heart was straightforward, but its result added little beyond confirming the clearly marked pump slot.

surprise.text: I was interested that red blood cells make ATP from sugar despite having no mitochondria, unlike the muscle cells built earlier.

arbitrary.text: No action felt particularly arbitrary; the pictures and slot labels gave the combinations clear purposes.

continue.text: I would continue to see how the circulation connects with other body systems. The tissue-exchange picture suggests useful next questions about where oxygen and nutrients enter the blood.
